$comment: Street-name normalisation rules, French — SPEC.md §4.3.
One file per language, in this directory, and the language is the one the
ADDRESS BASE is written in, not the one the interface speaks: an index
built over Antwerp is searched in Dutch whatever the phone is set to. The
index says which file it was built with (§15.1), so the two can never be
paired wrongly.
This file is the SINGLE SOURCE of the French rules. It is read by the index
generation script (tools/build_address_index.py) AND embedded in the APK,
where the search engine reads it again. A divergence between the two would
make streets unfindable: "boulevard" indexed on one side, "bd" searched
on the other, and no result. Hence the shared file rather than two copied
lists.
Normalisation is applied identically to the index and to what is typed:
lower case, letters folded, accents and punctuation removed, abbreviations
expanded.
tools/build_address_index.py also produces a set of reference cases that
the Kotlin test replays, to prove that the two implementations give the
same result. tools/refresh_normalization_fixtures.py recomputes them
whenever these rules change, without rebuilding the indexes. The names it
replays are "referenceNames" at the foot of this file.
SCOPE. The rules cover the whole of the French address base, mainland and
overseas: the application serves every conurbation publishing its stations
(§1), and a rule set written for one city leaves the others' streets
unfindable. The vocabulary of a Marseille traverse, a Lyon montée, a Breton
venelle and a Réunion ravine is as necessary here as the rue and the
boulevard.
Expanded during normalisation, on whole words only.
A single-letter abbreviation is expanded only at the head of a name,
otherwise "r" would turn "Jean R Dupont" into "Jean rue Dupont".
The bulk of the list is the DGFiP's table of way types, the one the
Base Adresse Nationale inherits from FANTOIR: those codes are what the
source data actually holds, so expanding them is what makes an indexed
name and a typed name meet.
Deliberately absent: "col", which is a mountain pass far more often
than it is a colonel, and "m", "mr", "mme", too common inside a name
to be safely rewritten.
The street type is stored in a field SEPARATE from the proper name
(§4.3): "gambetta" must find "rue Gambetta", and "rue de la gare" must
not be penalised by word order.
Recognised only at the head of a name, and by longest match: "rond
point" before "rond", "chemin rural" before "chemin".
Written in their already normalised form (no accent, lower case).
The list is national on purpose. A conurbation names its ways in its own
words, and the application serves any of them: "traverse" and "vallon"
are Marseille, "montee" and "traboule" are Lyon, "couree" and "dreve"
are the North, "venelle" and "hent" are Brittany, "cavee" is Normandy,
"carriera" and "cami" are the Occitan south, "ravine", "morne" and
"habitation" are the West Indies and Réunion. Leaving a region's
vocabulary out costs its inhabitants the type/name split, and with it
the ability to find a street by its proper name alone.

$letterReplacementsComment: Letters that survive accent removal, because they are not an accented
letter at all: NFD decomposition has nothing to take off a ligature. They
are folded here instead, on both sides of the search alike, so that
"Cœur de Ville" is found by whoever types "coeur".
$punctuationComment: Turned into word breaks on both sides of the search. The non-breaking
spaces are here rather than left to the whitespace split: Python treats
them as whitespace and Kotlin's \s does not, so a name holding one would
be indexed as two words and searched as one.

$comment: Stop words ignored when RANKING — never when indexing, otherwise
"rue de la gare" would lose half its content. They serve not to reward
a match that only bears on "de" or "la".

$referenceNamesComment: Names written out on purpose, replayed by the Kotlin test against every
network generated in this language. They exist because the real street
names sampled from a city's own address base only ever cover that city's
vocabulary: the first block is what any French address base holds, the
second is what a single region holds and the others do not. A rule added
for Marseille or for Saint-Denis de La Réunion is worth nothing if no test
ever reads a name written the way people write it there.
